learn.hook: In 2006, scientists voted that Pluto is no longer a full planet. Did Pluto change, or did our knowledge change?
points: Science is a way of finding out how the world works by observing, asking questions and testing ideas.
Scientific ideas are based on evidence. When strong new evidence appears, scientists improve or replace old ideas.
New tools like the telescope and the microscope let people see things they could never see before, so science grows.
Long ago many people believed the Earth was the centre of everything. Careful observations later showed that the Earth and other planets go around the Sun.
Science is never 'finished'. Every answer leads to new questions.

example.q: A student says, 'If scientists keep changing their ideas, science must be unreliable.' Is that right?
steps: Ask: why do scientists change an idea? Because new evidence is found.
Changing an idea to fit better evidence makes our knowledge more accurate, not less.
So the habit of checking and correcting is the strength of science.
example.answer: No. Science changes because it follows evidence, and that makes it more reliable over time.

learn.reallife: Weather forecasts on TV keep getting better because scientists keep improving their models with new satellite data.

games.title: Science facts check
items: Scientific ideas can change when new evidence is found.
Science follows evidence, so better evidence can update an idea.
Once something is written in a science book, it can never be improved.
Science keeps growing; books get updated when knowledge improves.
The microscope helped people discover tiny living cells.
Robert Hooke saw tiny box-like cells in cork through a microscope in 1665.
Pluto was reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006.
Astronomers placed Pluto in the new group 'dwarf planets' in 2006.
Only adults with lab coats can do science.
Anyone who observes carefully, asks questions and tests ideas is doing science.

games.title: How an idea in science improves
items: Scientists hold an idea based on what they know
New observations do not fit the idea
Scientists test and check the new evidence carefully
The idea is improved or replaced

quiz.q: What makes scientists change an accepted idea?
options: A popular vote of the public
quiz.explain: Scientific ideas stand or fall on evidence. When careful new observations or experiments disagree with an idea, it is improved.
quiz.mistake: Thinks ideas in science change because of opinion or age, not evidence

quiz.q: Which tool first let people see the craters on the Moon and the moons of Jupiter?
quiz.explain: A telescope makes far-away objects look nearer and larger. Galileo used one to see the Moon's craters and moons going around Jupiter.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the telescope (for far objects) with the microscope (for tiny objects)

quiz.q: Robert Hooke looked at a thin slice of cork under a microscope. What did he discover?
quiz.explain: In 1665 Hooke saw small boxes in cork and called them 'cells'. This opened up the study of the tiny units of life.
quiz.mistake: Thinks early microscopes could show atoms

quiz.q: Long ago, many people believed that the Sun goes around the Earth. What do we know now?
options: The Earth goes around the Sun
The Sun goes around the Earth
The Moon goes around the Sun only
quiz.explain: Careful observations showed that the Earth and other planets revolve around the Sun. The Sun only seems to move because the Earth spins.
quiz.mistake: Trusts how things look (the Sun seems to move) over evidence

quiz.q: Pluto is now called a dwarf planet. What does this example show about science?
options: Scientists made a mistake on purpose
Scientists update how they group things as they learn more
quiz.explain: Pluto did not change. As astronomers found many similar objects, they made clearer rules for what counts as a planet.
quiz.mistake: Thinks reclassifying means the object itself changed

quiz.q: Which statement about science is correct?
options: Science is a process that keeps growing
Science is a fixed list of facts to memorise
Science only happens in big laboratories
Science answers are decided by the oldest scientist
quiz.explain: Science is a way of finding out. It grows as people ask new questions and test them.
quiz.mistake: Sees science as only a set of facts rather than a way of finding out

quiz.q: Why do scientists share their results with other scientists?
options: So no one else can use the idea
Because sharing is required only for prizes
So others can check and repeat the work
quiz.explain: Other scientists repeating an experiment and getting the same result makes us more confident it is right.
quiz.mistake: Does not know that checking by others is part of science

quiz.q: Earlier, people thought heavy and light objects always fall at very different speeds. Experiments showed that, without air in the way, they fall together. This shows that:
options: Testing can correct a common belief
Air has no effect at all on falling
quiz.explain: A careful test showed that air resistance, not weight, causes most of the difference. The old belief was corrected by evidence.
quiz.mistake: Accepts everyday beliefs without testing them

teach.ask: Chirp! Gappu read that scientists changed their minds about Pluto. Does that mean science is wrong? How does science grow?
teach.praise: Tweet! Science changes when the evidence changes. That's a superpower, not a weakness!
teach.nudge: But what makes a scientist change an old idea?

learn.hook: India celebrates National Science Day every year on 28 February. Can you guess which discovery it remembers?
points: People from every part of the world, including India, have added to science.
C.V. Raman discovered how light scatters in a special way (the Raman effect) on 28 February 1928 and won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1930.
Jagadish Chandra Bose built a very sensitive instrument, the crescograph, to measure the tiny growth of plants.
Scientists build on each other's work. One discovery often makes the next one possible.
Today science is often done by big teams, like the ISRO team whose Chandrayaan-3 lander touched down near the Moon's south pole on 23 August 2023.

example.q: Why did Chandrayaan-3 need people who knew maths, chemistry, physics, computers and more?
steps: A Moon mission needs rockets (physics), fuel (chemistry), path calculations (maths) and control programs (computers).
No single person knows all of this well enough.
So people with different skills work as one team, using knowledge built by many people before them.
example.answer: Because big science problems need many kinds of knowledge working together.

learn.reallife: The mobile phone in your home uses ideas from physics, chemistry, maths and engineering, discovered by people from many countries over hundreds of years.

games.title: Match the scientist to the work

items.text: National Science Day in India is on 28 ___.
C.V. Raman won the Nobel Prize in ___ in 1930.
Chandrayaan-3 landed near the Moon's ___ pole.
Salim Ali is known as the Birdman of ___.

quiz.q: On which date is National Science Day celebrated in India?
quiz.explain: It marks the day in 1928 when C.V. Raman announced the discovery of the Raman effect.
quiz.mistake: Mixes it up with other well-known days such as Children's Day or Teachers' Day

quiz.q: In which year did C.V. Raman win the Nobel Prize in Physics?
quiz.explain: He discovered the Raman effect in 1928 and was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1930.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the year of the discovery (1928) with the year of the prize

quiz.q: What did Jagadish Chandra Bose's crescograph measure?
options: The very small growth of plants
quiz.explain: The crescograph magnified tiny movements, showing how plants grow and respond to things around them.
quiz.mistake: Guesses from the sound of the name instead of knowing the instrument

quiz.q: Who is known as the 'Birdman of India'?
quiz.explain: Salim Ali spent his life studying and writing about the birds of India.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up famous Indian scientists and their fields

quiz.q: Chandrayaan-3's lander touched down near the Moon's south pole on which date?
quiz.explain: Chandrayaan-3 was launched on 14 July 2023 and landed on 23 August 2023. India now marks 23 August as National Space Day.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the launch date with the landing date

quiz.q: Edward Jenner is remembered for which discovery?
quiz.explain: In 1796 Jenner showed that a mild cowpox infection could protect people from smallpox. This was the start of vaccines.
quiz.mistake: Does not connect Jenner with vaccines

quiz.q: Why is it said that science is built 'on the shoulders' of earlier scientists?
options: Only one person makes each discovery from nothing
Each discovery uses knowledge found earlier
quiz.explain: New discoveries use tools, facts and ideas worked out earlier by others. Science is a chain of shared work.
quiz.mistake: Thinks each discovery is made alone, without earlier knowledge

quiz.q: A big Moon mission needs experts in rockets, fuel, computers and maths. What does this show?
options: Only one subject matters in science
Big science needs teamwork across subjects
quiz.explain: Rockets need physics, fuel needs chemistry, the path needs maths and control needs computers. Teams combine all of these.
quiz.mistake: Thinks science subjects are separate and never work together

teach.ask: Gappu wants to know: is science done by just one genius sitting alone? Who adds to science?
teach.praise: Tweet tweet! Science is a giant team game played by people everywhere, including India!
teach.nudge: Can you name an Indian scientist and what they found?

learn.hook: Why does a steel tumbler of cold water 'sweat' on a hot day? Every great discovery starts with a 'why' like this!
points: Curiosity means wanting to know. Inquiry means finding out step by step.
The steps: observe, ask a question, make a guess you can test (a hypothesis), test it with an experiment, record results, draw a conclusion.
In a fair test you change only one thing (the variable you are testing) and keep everything else the same.
Record what really happens, even if it is different from what you expected.
Repeat the test to be sure your result is not just luck.

example.q: Meena wants to test whether salt helps ice melt faster. She puts salt on one ice cube in the sun and no salt on another ice cube in the shade. Is this a fair test?
steps: List what is different: salt and also sun versus shade.
Two things are changed, so we cannot tell which one made the ice melt faster.
Make it fair: keep both cubes the same size and in the same place; change only the salt.
example.answer: Not fair. She should change only one thing, the salt, and keep everything else the same.

learn.reallife: Your doctor uses inquiry too: noticing symptoms, guessing the cause, ordering a test and then deciding the treatment.

games.title: Steps of a science inquiry
items: Observe something interesting
Ask a question
Make a testable guess (hypothesis)
Do a fair test and record results
Draw a conclusion

games.title: Testable or not testable?
buckets: Can be tested by an experiment
Cannot be tested by an experiment
items: Does a plant grow taller in sunlight than in shade?
Does warm water dissolve sugar faster than cold water?
Which colour is the most beautiful?
Does a heavier ball roll farther down a ramp?
Is mango tastier than chikoo?
Which song is the best?

quiz.q: What is a hypothesis?
options: The final answer of an experiment
A guess that can be tested
A wild guess that cannot be checked
quiz.explain: A hypothesis is an idea you can test, such as 'Plants kept in sunlight will grow taller'. The experiment checks it.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a hypothesis is the result instead of the starting guess

quiz.q: Arjun tests whether sunlight helps plants grow. Which is the ONE thing he should change?
quiz.explain: In a fair test you change only the factor you are testing. Water, pot and plant type must stay the same.
quiz.mistake: Changes many things at once, so the result can't be trusted

quiz.q: In an experiment the result is different from what you predicted. What should you do?
options: Record the real result and think about why
Change the result to match the guess
quiz.explain: Honest recording is the heart of science. Surprising results often lead to new discoveries.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a 'wrong' prediction means the experiment failed

quiz.q: Why should an experiment be repeated a few times?
options: Because the first try is always wrong
To check that the result was not just luck
quiz.explain: If you get the same result again and again, you can be more confident it is real.
quiz.mistake: Thinks one result is enough to be sure

quiz.q: Which question can be answered by a science experiment?
options: Is blue a nicer colour than green?
Does salt water freeze at a lower temperature than plain water?
quiz.explain: Freezing temperature can be measured. The other questions are about likes and opinions.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up opinion questions with questions that can be measured

quiz.q: Riya notices ants walking in a line to a sugar spill. This first step of inquiry is called:
quiz.explain: Noticing something carefully with your senses is observation. It usually comes first and leads to a question.
quiz.mistake: Does not know the names of the steps of inquiry

quiz.q: Kabir drops a paper ball and a flat sheet of paper from the same height at the same time. What is the fair-test idea here?
options: Same paper and same height; only the shape is changed
Using a stone instead of paper
quiz.explain: Keeping the paper and height the same means only the shape can explain any difference in falling time.
quiz.mistake: Does not see which factors must be kept the same

quiz.q: Which of these is a conclusion?
options: I wonder if plants need sunlight
I will put one pot in a cupboard
I need two pots and soil
Plants kept in sunlight grew taller than those kept in a dark cupboard
quiz.explain: A conclusion states what the results show. The other options are a question, a plan and a list of materials.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the question or the plan with the conclusion

teach.ask: Gappu wants to be a scientist! How should Gappu find out the answer to a 'why' question?
teach.praise: Chirp chirp! Observe, ask, guess, test, conclude. Gappu is ready to be a scientist!
teach.nudge: How will Gappu check if the guess is right?

chapters.title: Exploring Substances: Acidic, Basic, and Neutral

learn.hook: Nimbu pani, imli chutney and dahi all taste sour. Is there a hidden science reason?
points: Acids usually taste sour. The word 'acid' comes from the Latin word 'acere', meaning sour.
Bases usually taste bitter and feel soapy or slippery when touched.
Substances that are neither acidic nor basic are called neutral, like sugar solution, common salt solution and pure water.
Food acids: lemon and orange have citric acid, curd has lactic acid, vinegar has acetic acid, tamarind has tartaric acid and amla has ascorbic acid (vitamin C).
Safety first: never taste or touch unknown substances in a lab. Some acids and bases are strong enough to burn skin.

example.q: Soap solution feels slippery between the fingers and tastes bitter (please don't try!). Is it acidic, basic or neutral?
steps: Acids are sour; bases are bitter and soapy to touch.
Soap solution feels soapy and is bitter.
So it matches the properties of a base.
example.answer: Soap solution is basic.

learn.reallife: The sour taste of raw mango and the fizz in lemon with baking soda both come from acids at work in your kitchen.

games.title: Acidic, basic or neutral?
items: Lemon juice
Vinegar
Curd
Soap solution
Lime water
Baking soda solution
Sugar solution
Common salt solution
Pure water

games.title: Match the food to its acid

quiz.q: Which acid is found in curd?
quiz.explain: Bacteria turn milk into curd and make lactic acid, which gives curd its sour taste.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the names of acids found in different foods

quiz.q: Vinegar, used in pickles and salads, contains mainly which acid?
quiz.explain: Vinegar is a dilute solution of acetic acid in water.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up vinegar with curd or tamarind

quiz.q: How do bases usually feel when touched (when diluted and safe)?
quiz.explain: Bases feel soapy. 'Sour' is a taste, not a feel, and it belongs to acids.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the properties of acids and bases

quiz.q: Which of these is a neutral substance?
quiz.explain: Sugar solution does not change the colour of litmus, so it is neutral. Lemon juice is acidic; soap and lime water are basic.
quiz.mistake: Thinks anything sweet or tasty must be acidic

quiz.q: Amla is a rich source of vitamin C. What is the chemical name of vitamin C?
quiz.explain: Vitamin C is ascorbic acid. It is found in amla, oranges, guava and many fruits.
quiz.mistake: Thinks all sour fruits only contain citric acid

quiz.q: Why should you never taste chemicals in a science lab to find out if they are acids?
options: Some acids and bases can burn or poison you
quiz.explain: Strong acids and bases can harm the mouth and skin. Scientists use indicators instead of tasting.
quiz.mistake: Thinks all acids are as mild as lemon juice

quiz.q: Lime water is made by dissolving which substance in water?
quiz.explain: Lime water is a solution of calcium hydroxide. It is a base.
quiz.mistake: Thinks lime water is made from lime (nimbu) fruit juice

quiz.q: Which pair has one acid and one base?
quiz.explain: Lemon juice is acidic and soap solution is basic. Vinegar and curd are both acids; soap and lime water are both bases; salt and sugar solutions are neutral.
quiz.mistake: Groups substances without checking each one

teach.ask: Gappu tasted lemon and it was sour! How can Gappu tell acids, bases and neutral things apart?
teach.praise: Tweet! Sour acids, bitter soapy bases and neutral in between. Gappu gets it!
teach.nudge: What about things that are neither acid nor base? What are they called?

learn.hook: A yellow haldi stain on your school shirt turns red when you scrub it with soap. Magic? No, chemistry!
points: An indicator is a substance that shows by changing colour whether something is acidic, basic or neutral.
Litmus comes from lichens. Acids turn blue litmus red. Bases turn red litmus blue. Neutral solutions change neither.
Turmeric (haldi) is yellow. It turns red in a base and stays yellow in an acid or a neutral solution.
China rose (gudhal or hibiscus) petal extract turns dark pink (magenta) in an acid and green in a base.
Indicators are safer than tasting, so they are the scientist's tool for testing.

example.q: A clear liquid turns red litmus blue. It does not change blue litmus. What is it, and what will turmeric paper do in it?
steps: Red litmus turning blue means the liquid is a base.
Bases do not change blue litmus, which matches.
Turmeric turns red in a base.
example.answer: It is a base, and turmeric paper will turn red.

learn.reallife: When you wash a turmeric (haldi) curry stain with soap, it turns red because soap is basic. After rinsing well with plenty of water, it turns yellow again.

games.title: Indicator check
items: Litmus is obtained from lichens.
Lichens are small living things that grow on rocks and tree bark. Litmus dye is taken from them.
Acids turn red litmus blue.
Acids turn blue litmus red. Bases turn red litmus blue.
Turmeric turns red in soap solution.
Soap solution is basic, and turmeric turns red in a base.
A neutral solution changes blue litmus to red.
A neutral solution does not change the colour of either red or blue litmus.
China rose extract turns green in a basic solution.
China rose indicator turns green in bases and dark pink in acids.
Turmeric turns red in lemon juice.
Lemon juice is acidic, and turmeric stays yellow in acids.

quiz.q: What colour does blue litmus turn in lemon juice?
quiz.explain: Lemon juice is acidic, and acids turn blue litmus red.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the colour change of acids and bases

quiz.q: A solution turns turmeric paper red. The solution is:
quiz.explain: Turmeric changes from yellow to red only in bases.
quiz.mistake: Thinks red always means acid, as it does for blue litmus

quiz.q: Litmus is obtained from:
quiz.explain: Litmus dye comes from lichens. Rose and turmeric give other natural indicators.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the sources of natural indicators

quiz.q: Salt solution is tested with red and blue litmus. What happens?
quiz.explain: Common salt solution is neutral, so it changes neither red nor blue litmus.
quiz.mistake: Thinks every solution must change litmus in some way

quiz.q: China rose extract is added to vinegar. What colour appears?
quiz.explain: Vinegar is acidic. China rose indicator turns dark pink (magenta) in acids and green in bases.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the colours of China rose in acid and base

quiz.q: Why is red litmus alone not enough to tell an acid from a neutral solution?
options: Red litmus turns blue in acids
Red litmus turns green in neutral solutions
Red litmus stays red in both
quiz.explain: Red litmus changes only in a base. To spot an acid you need blue litmus, which turns red in acids.
quiz.mistake: Thinks one litmus colour can detect all three kinds of substances

quiz.q: What is an indicator?
options: A substance that makes acids stronger
A substance that changes colour in acids or bases
quiz.explain: Indicators show whether a substance is acidic, basic or neutral by their colour change.
quiz.mistake: Confuses an indicator with an acid or with a measuring instrument

quiz.q: Which of these would turn red litmus blue?
quiz.explain: Baking soda solution is basic, and bases turn red litmus blue. Orange juice and vinegar are acids; sugar solution is neutral.
quiz.mistake: Does not remember that baking soda is a base

teach.ask: Gappu found red and blue paper strips in the lab. How can these colours tell Gappu if something is an acid or a base?
teach.praise: Wow! Blue to red means acid, red to blue means base. Gappu is a colour detective now!
teach.nudge: What happens to blue litmus when it meets an acid?

learn.hook: An ant bite stings because the ant injects an acid. What could cancel the sting?
points: When an acid and a base react, they cancel each other's effect. This is called neutralisation.
Acid + base gives salt + water, and heat is given out.
In neutralisation, 'salt' means a new substance formed from the acid and the base. Common salt is only one example.
Antacids such as milk of magnesia (a base) are used to relieve acidity in the stomach.
Ant bites contain formic acid. Rubbing moist baking soda or calamine solution (both mildly basic) on them helps.

example.q: A farmer finds that the soil in his field is too acidic for his crops. What should he add, and why?
steps: Acidic soil needs a base to neutralise it.
Quicklime (calcium oxide) or slaked lime (calcium hydroxide) are bases.
Adding them neutralises the extra acid, so the crops can grow better.
example.answer: He should add quicklime or slaked lime, which are bases that neutralise the acid in the soil.

learn.reallife: If soil is too basic, farmers add organic matter like compost, which releases acids. Factories must neutralise acidic waste water with bases before letting it out.

games.title: Steps of a safe neutralisation activity (with a teacher)
items: Take a little dilute acid in a test tube
Add two or three drops of an indicator
Add a base drop by drop while gently shaking
Watch for the colour change that shows the acid is neutralised
Feel the outside of the tube: it is slightly warm

games.title: Which do you add to neutralise it?
buckets: Add an acid or acidic material
items: Ant bite (formic acid)
Too much acid in the stomach
Acidic soil
Acidic factory waste
Soil that is too basic
Basic waste water from a factory

quiz.q: What are the products when an acid reacts with a base?
quiz.explain: Neutralisation forms a salt and water, and heat is also given out.
quiz.mistake: Forgets that a new substance (salt) forms along with water

quiz.q: Milk of magnesia is taken for acidity. It works because it is:
options: A base that neutralises extra stomach acid
An acid that adds more acid
A sugar that coats the stomach
quiz.explain: Milk of magnesia contains magnesium hydroxide, a base. It neutralises extra acid in the stomach.
quiz.mistake: Thinks antacids work by adding acid or by just diluting

quiz.q: An ant sting contains which acid?
quiz.explain: Ants inject formic acid, which causes the burning feeling.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the acids found in living things and foods

quiz.q: Which is used to treat an ant bite?
quiz.explain: Baking soda is a mild base and neutralises the formic acid. Vinegar, lemon and tamarind are acids and would not help.
quiz.mistake: Picks another acid instead of a base

quiz.q: During neutralisation, the test tube becomes slightly warm. Why?
options: Heat is given out in the reaction
quiz.explain: Neutralisation releases heat, so the mixture warms up.
quiz.mistake: Does not know that neutralisation gives out heat

quiz.q: Soil in a field is too basic. What should the farmer add?
quiz.explain: Compost releases acids that neutralise the extra base. Quicklime, slaked lime and baking soda are bases and would make it worse.
quiz.mistake: Adds lime to every soil problem without checking if the soil is acidic or basic

quiz.q: Why must factories treat acidic waste before releasing it into rivers?
options: The acid can harm fish and plants in the water
Acid makes the river water sweet
Fish need extra acid to grow
quiz.explain: Acidic waste harms living things in water. Adding a base neutralises it first.
quiz.mistake: Does not connect acids in water with harm to living things

quiz.q: In science, the word 'salt' in 'acid + base gives salt + water' means:
options: A new substance formed from the acid and base
quiz.explain: Different acids and bases form different salts. Common salt (sodium chloride) is just one of them.
quiz.mistake: Thinks every salt is table salt

teach.ask: Gappu has a stomach ache from eating too many spicy pakoras! The doctor gives an antacid. How does it help?
teach.praise: Tweet tweet! The base in the antacid neutralises the extra acid. Gappu's tummy feels better!
teach.nudge: What does an acid and a base make when they react?

learn.hook: A tiny torch cell has no wires to the wall, yet it can light a bulb. Where does its electricity come from?
points: An electric cell makes electricity from chemicals stored inside it. When the chemicals are used up, the cell stops working.
Every cell has two terminals: a positive (+) terminal, the metal cap, and a negative (−) terminal, the flat metal disc.
A torch bulb has a thin coiled wire called the filament. It glows when electricity flows through it. If the filament breaks, the bulb is 'fused'.
An LED (light emitting diode) has two wires. The longer one goes to the positive side. An LED glows only when connected the right way round.
A switch is a simple device that joins (ON) or breaks (OFF) the path of electricity.

example.q: Raju connects a bulb to a new cell correctly, but it does not glow. Another bulb glows in the same set-up. What is wrong with the first bulb?
steps: The cell is new and works, because another bulb glows.
So the problem is in the first bulb.
Look at its filament: if it is broken, electricity cannot pass through.
example.answer: The first bulb is fused: its filament is broken.

learn.reallife: Torches, TV remotes, wall clocks and toys run on cells. Joining two or more cells together makes a battery, like the one in a mobile phone.

games.title: Match the part to its job
Cell and bulb facts
items: The metal cap of a cell is its positive terminal.
The cap is marked + and the flat disc is −.
A fused bulb has a broken filament.
With the filament broken, the path for electricity is broken.
An LED glows whichever way you connect it.
An LED lets electricity pass only one way, so it must be connected the right way round.
A battery is made by joining two or more cells.
Cells joined + to − make a battery that can give more electricity.
You can safely open a cell to see the chemicals inside.
Cells contain chemicals that can harm you. Never open, burn or break them.

quiz.q: Which part of a torch bulb glows?
quiz.explain: The filament is a thin coiled wire that becomes hot and glows when current passes through it.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the glass itself makes the light

quiz.q: What is the metal cap on top of a cell called?
quiz.explain: The metal cap is the positive (+) terminal. The flat metal disc at the bottom is the negative (−) terminal.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the positive and negative terminals

quiz.q: Where does a torch cell (dry cell) get its electricity from?
quiz.explain: A cell turns stored chemical energy into electricity. When these chemicals are used up, the cell has to be replaced or recharged.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the cell is charged by air or light

quiz.q: An LED does not glow even though the cell is new. What is the most likely reason?
options: It is connected the wrong way round
quiz.explain: An LED glows only when its longer leg is connected towards the positive terminal. Turning it around fixes the problem.
quiz.mistake: Does not know that an LED works only in one direction

quiz.q: What is a battery?
options: Two or more cells joined together
quiz.explain: In a battery the positive terminal of one cell is joined to the negative terminal of the next.
quiz.mistake: Thinks 'battery' and 'cell' always mean the same thing

quiz.q: What does a switch do in a circuit?
options: It joins or breaks the path of electricity
It makes the bulb brighter forever
quiz.explain: In the ON position the switch completes the path; in the OFF position it breaks it.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a switch is a source of electricity

quiz.q: Which of these is a safe habit?
options: Open old cells to see inside
Put cells in a fire to get rid of them
Touch wires of a wall socket
Never open, burn or play with cells
quiz.explain: Cells contain chemicals, and wall sockets carry dangerous electricity. Old cells should be given for proper disposal.
quiz.mistake: Does not see the danger in cells and sockets

quiz.q: Why does a torch stop glowing after being used for many weeks?
options: The chemicals in its cells are used up
quiz.explain: As the cell works, its chemicals get used up. Then it can no longer push electricity through the bulb.
quiz.mistake: Thinks cells hold electricity that never runs out

teach.ask: Gappu found a torch cell and a little bulb. What are these parts and how does a cell make the bulb light up?
teach.praise: Chirp! The cell's chemicals push electricity through the filament and it glows. Bright idea, Gappu!

learn.hook: Electricity is like a racing track: it only flows if the track is a complete loop with no gaps!
points: A circuit is a complete, closed path for electricity: from the positive terminal of the cell, through wires and a bulb, back to the negative terminal.
If there is any gap, the circuit is open (or broken) and the bulb does not glow.
A switch in the ON position closes the circuit. In the OFF position it opens it.
Scientists draw circuits using symbols. In a cell symbol, the longer thin line is the positive terminal and the shorter thick line is the negative terminal.
A circuit diagram is quick to draw and easy for anyone in the world to read.

example.q: A bulb is joined to a cell with two wires, but both wires touch only the positive terminal. Will the bulb glow?
steps: For the bulb to glow, electricity must flow through a complete loop.
The loop must go from the positive terminal, through the bulb, to the negative terminal.
Here the negative terminal is not connected, so the path is not complete.
example.answer: No. The circuit is open, because the negative terminal is not connected.

learn.reallife: When you press the switch of a fan at home, you complete a circuit. Electricians read circuit diagrams to wire buildings safely.

learn.hook: Why does the screwdriver of an electrician have a plastic or rubber handle? Let's find out!
points: Materials that let electricity pass through them easily are called conductors. Metals like copper, aluminium and iron are good conductors.
Materials that do not let electricity pass easily are called insulators, like rubber, plastic, dry wood, glass and dry paper.
Graphite (the 'lead' of a pencil) is not a metal, but it conducts electricity.
Wires have a copper or aluminium core covered with a plastic coat. The metal carries the current; the plastic keeps us safe.
Our body can conduct electricity, so never touch switches with wet hands or play near electric poles. The mains supply in Indian homes is about 230 volts, which is dangerous.

example.q: You make a tester: a cell, a bulb and two wires with a gap. You touch both free ends to a steel spoon and the bulb glows. Then you try a plastic ruler and it does not. What do you conclude?
steps: The bulb glows only if the object completes the circuit.
The steel spoon completed it: it lets current pass.
The plastic ruler did not: it blocks current.
example.answer: Steel (a metal) is a conductor; plastic is an insulator.

learn.reallife: Electricians wear rubber gloves and rubber-soled shoes, and switch boards are made of plastic, because these are insulators.

chapters.title: The World of Metals and Non-metals

learn.hook: The silver vark on a kaju katli is a metal sheet beaten so thin that you can eat it! How can a metal become that thin?
points: Lustre: metals have a shiny surface, especially when freshly cut or polished.
Malleable: metals can be beaten into thin sheets, like aluminium foil and silver vark.
Ductile: metals can be drawn into thin wires, like copper wires.
Sonorous: metals make a ringing sound when struck, which is why bells are made of metal.
Metals are good conductors of heat and electricity. Most are hard, but sodium and potassium are so soft they can be cut with a knife, and mercury is a liquid at room temperature.

example.q: A shopkeeper hammers a lump of material and it spreads into a thin sheet without breaking. Then he taps it and it rings. Is it more likely a metal or a non-metal?
steps: Spreading into a sheet when hammered is called malleability.
Ringing when struck is called sonority.
Both are typical properties of metals.
example.answer: It is most likely a metal.

learn.reallife: A steel tiffin, copper wires in your house, a brass temple bell and aluminium foil around rotis all use special properties of metals.

learn.hook: Diamond, the hardest natural substance, and pencil 'lead' are both made of the same non-metal: carbon!
points: Non-metals are usually dull, not sonorous and poor conductors of heat and electricity.
Solid non-metals like sulphur and coal are brittle: they break or turn to powder when hammered.
Many non-metals are gases, such as oxygen, nitrogen, hydrogen and chlorine. Bromine is a liquid non-metal.
Exceptions: iodine is a shiny non-metal, graphite conducts electricity, and diamond is very hard.
When metals burn in air they form oxides that are basic (they turn red litmus blue). Oxides of non-metals like sulphur are acidic (they turn blue litmus red).

example.q: In a teacher's demonstration, a magnesium ribbon burns with a bright white light and leaves white ash. The ash is dissolved in water and tested with litmus. Which litmus changes, and why?
steps: Magnesium is a metal, so its ash is magnesium oxide, a metal oxide.
Metal oxides make basic solutions.
Bases turn red litmus blue.
example.answer: Red litmus turns blue, because magnesium oxide forms a basic solution.

learn.hook: From the iron in railway tracks to the oxygen cylinders in hospitals, metals and non-metals keep India running!

Copper and aluminium make electric wires; aluminium also makes foil, utensils and aeroplane parts because it is light.
Gold and silver are used in jewellery because they are lustrous and malleable, and gold keeps its shine for a very long time; silver is also beaten into vark for sweets.
Oxygen is needed for breathing; nitrogen is used to make fertilisers and to fill food packets; chlorine is used to clean drinking water.
Carbon (as graphite) is used in pencils, and iodine is used as an antiseptic on wounds.

example.q: Why is the handle of a cooking pan made of wood or plastic, while the pan is made of metal?
steps: The pan must pass heat to the food, so it needs a good conductor: a metal.
The handle must not get hot, so it needs a poor conductor.
Wood and plastic are poor conductors of heat.

chapters.title: Changes Around Us: Physical and Chemical

learn.hook: You can melt ghee and set it again, but can you ever 'unfry' a puri? That is the difference between two kinds of change!
points: A physical change alters the shape, size or state of a substance, but no new substance is formed. Examples: melting ice, dissolving sugar, tearing paper.
Many physical changes can be reversed, but not all: torn paper stays torn, yet it is still paper.
A chemical change forms one or more new substances. Examples: burning, cooking, rusting, curdling of milk, ripening of fruit.
Signs of a chemical change: a gas is given off, the colour changes, heat or light is produced, or a new smell appears.
Some events have both: when a candle burns, the wax melts (physical) and also burns (chemical).

example.q: Your teacher adds a spoon of baking soda to vinegar. It fizzes. When the gas is passed into lime water, the lime water turns milky. Is this a physical or a chemical change?
steps: Fizzing shows a gas is being made.
The gas is carbon dioxide; it turns lime water milky by forming a new substance.
New substances are formed, so it is a chemical change.
example.answer: It is a chemical change: new substances such as carbon dioxide are formed.

learn.reallife: Making dahi from milk, cooking dal, burning a diya and fruits ripening are chemical changes. Melting butter, making ice in the freezer and dissolving sugar in tea are physical changes.

learn.hook: The Iron Pillar in Delhi has stood for more than 1,600 years with very little rust. Yet a bicycle left in the rain gets rusty in weeks!
points: Rusting is a chemical change in which iron reacts with oxygen (from air) and water (or moisture) to form rust, a reddish-brown substance (iron oxide).
Both air and water are needed for rusting. Without either one, iron does not rust.
Rusting is faster in humid places and near the sea, where the air is moist and salty.
Rust is flaky. It falls off and exposes fresh iron, so the iron slowly gets eaten away.
We prevent rusting by painting, oiling or greasing, and by galvanisation (coating iron with zinc). Stainless steel, made by mixing iron with metals like chromium and nickel, does not rust easily.

example.q: Three iron nails are kept: A in dry air (with a drying agent), B in boiled water covered with an oil layer, and C in a test tube with a little water and open to air. Which nail rusts?
steps: A has air but no water.
B has water but the oil layer and boiling keep air out.
C has both air and water.
example.answer: Only nail C rusts, because rusting needs both air and water.

learn.hook: Mishri, the crystal sugar many families enjoy with saunf after meals, is made by a process called crystallisation!
points: Crystals are solids with regular shapes and flat, shiny faces. Salt, sugar, alum (phitkari) and copper sulphate form crystals.
Crystallisation is a way to get large, pure crystals of a substance from its solution.
Steps: dissolve as much of the substance as possible in hot water, filter it, then let it cool slowly without disturbing it.
Hot water can dissolve more of a substance than cold water, so crystals appear as the solution cools.
Crystallisation is a physical change: the substance stays the same, only its form changes.

example.q: Salt can be got by drying sea water in the sun. Why do we need crystallisation to get pure salt?

chapters.title: Adolescence: A Stage of Growth and Change

learn.hook: Have you noticed that some classmates suddenly look taller after the summer holidays? Welcome to the growth spurt!
points: Adolescence is the stage of life between childhood and adulthood, the teenage years. The body and mind both change.
Puberty is the time when the body starts changing towards an adult body. It is controlled by hormones, chemical messengers made in the body.
Common changes: a sudden increase in height (growth spurt), new hair growth, more sweat and oil, and a changing voice.

In boys the voice box grows and the voice becomes deeper; it may crack for a while. A bump in the throat called the Adam's apple may show. In girls, the body shape changes and periods (menstruation) begin, which is a normal, healthy process.
Changes start at different ages for different people. Girls often begin a little earlier than boys. All of this is normal.

example.q: Aman is shorter than most of his friends in Class 7 and feels worried. What would you tell him?
steps: Puberty and the growth spurt start at different ages in different people.
Many children grow quickly a little later.
Height also depends on family genes, food, sleep and exercise.
example.answer: There is no need to worry: everyone has their own timing, and eating well, sleeping well and staying active help growth.

learn.reallife: Doctors and school health check-ups track height and weight to make sure children are growing in a healthy way.

learn.hook: Your body is like a new phone getting a big update during adolescence. It needs the right care to run smoothly!
points: More sweat and oil means you should bathe daily, wear clean, washed clothes and keep your hair clean.

Girls should use clean sanitary pads or clean cloth during periods, change them regularly, and wrap and throw them in a dustbin.
Eat a balanced diet: proteins for growth, calcium (milk, curd, ragi) for bones, and iron (green leafy vegetables, jaggery, pulses) for healthy blood.
Get enough sleep, play or exercise every day, and drink plenty of water. Avoid too much junk food and fizzy drinks.

learn.hook: Stir hot chai with a steel spoon and soon the handle feels hot, even though it never touched the tea. How did the heat travel up?
points: Heat always flows from a hotter object or part to a colder one.
In conduction, heat passes from particle to particle through a material, while the material itself stays in place. It is the main way heat moves through solids.
Materials that let heat pass easily are good conductors of heat, such as metals like steel, copper and aluminium.
Materials that do not let heat pass easily are poor conductors (insulators), such as wood, plastic, cloth, wool and air.
Woollen clothes keep us warm because wool traps air between its fibres, and air is a poor conductor of heat.

example.q: On a cold morning, an iron gate feels much colder than a wooden bench, though both are in the same place. Why?
steps: Both are at about the same temperature because they are in the same air.
Iron is a good conductor, so it quickly takes heat away from your warm hand.
Wood is a poor conductor, so heat leaves your hand slowly.
example.answer: Iron conducts heat away from the hand faster, so it feels colder, even though both are at about the same temperature.

learn.hook: Why do kitchen exhaust fans and ventilators sit high up near the ceiling, and how does the Sun's heat cross empty space to reach us?
points: In liquids and gases, heat moves mainly by convection: the warmer part becomes lighter and rises, and the cooler, heavier part moves down to take its place.
This up-and-down movement is called a convection current. You can see it when water is heated in a pan.
Radiation is the transfer of heat without needing any material in between. Heat from the Sun reaches the Earth through empty space by radiation.
We also feel radiation as warmth when we sit in front of a fire or a heater.
Dark-coloured surfaces absorb more heat; light-coloured surfaces reflect more. That is why white or light-coloured cotton clothes are comfortable in summer.

example.q: A room heater is placed on the floor, but an air conditioner is fixed high on the wall. Why?
steps: Warm air is lighter and rises, so warm air from a low heater spreads upward through the room.
Cool air is heavier and sinks, so cool air from a high AC spreads downward through the room.
Both placements use convection currents to mix the air in the whole room.
example.answer: Because warm air rises and cool air sinks, so these positions spread the heat or cool air through the room by convection.

learn.reallife: Solar water heaters on rooftops have black panels to absorb the Sun's radiation, and many houses in Rajasthan are painted in light colours to stay cooler.

learn.hook: At Marina Beach in Chennai, the breeze on a sunny afternoon comes from the sea. Late at night, it can come from the land. Why does it switch?
points: Land heats up faster than water during the day, and cools down faster at night.
Sea breeze (daytime): air above the hot land warms and rises. Cooler air from over the sea moves in to take its place, so wind blows from sea to land.
Land breeze (night): land becomes cooler than the sea. Air above the warmer sea rises, and cooler air from the land moves out to the sea.
Breezes are convection currents on a large scale: warm air rises and cooler air flows in.
These breezes make coastal places like Mumbai, Chennai and Kochi more pleasant.

example.q: It is 2 p.m. on a sunny day in Goa. Which way is the breeze blowing, and why?

Cooler air from the sea rushes in to replace it.
example.answer: From the sea towards the land: a sea breeze.

learn.hook: At Jantar Mantar in Jaipur stands a giant sundial, the Samrat Yantra, built by Maharaja Sawai Jai Singh II. Its shadow tells the time!
points: Long ago, people measured time using the Sun and natural events: the day, the phases of the Moon and the year.
Sundials use a moving shadow; sand clocks (hourglasses) use falling sand; water clocks, called ghatika in ancient India, used a bowl with a small hole that slowly filled and sank in water.
A simple pendulum is a small heavy ball (bob) hanging from a thread. One complete to-and-fro swing is one oscillation, and the time it takes is the time period.
For a pendulum of fixed length at a place, the time period stays the same. A longer thread gives a longer time period. That is why pendulums were used in clocks.
The basic (SI) unit of time is the second (s). 1 minute = 60 s, 1 hour = 60 minutes = 3600 s, and 1 day = 24 hours.

example.q: A pendulum makes 20 complete oscillations in 40 seconds. What is its time period?
steps: Time period = total time ÷ number of oscillations

learn.hook: A cheetah can sprint faster than a car on a city road, but a tortoise is happy to take its time. How do we compare how fast things move?
points: Speed tells us how much distance is covered in a unit of time.

The SI unit of speed is metre per second (m/s). For vehicles we often use kilometre per hour (km/h).
If an object covers equal distances in equal intervals of time along a straight line, its motion is uniform. Otherwise it is non-uniform, like a bus in city traffic.

learn.hook: A picture can tell a whole journey story! A distance-time graph shows at a glance whether someone was fast, slow or resting.
points: A distance-time graph shows time on the horizontal (x) axis and distance on the vertical (y) axis.

A flat (horizontal) line means the distance is not changing: the object is at rest.
A curved line means the speed is changing: non-uniform motion.

learn.hook: Chew a bite of roti for a long time and it starts tasting a little sweet. Your saliva is already doing chemistry!
points: Digestion breaks food down into simple substances that the body can absorb and use.
The path of food: mouth → food pipe (oesophagus) → stomach → small intestine → large intestine → rectum → anus.
In the mouth, teeth break food into small pieces and saliva starts turning starch into sugar. Incisors cut, canines tear, and premolars and molars grind.

The stomach makes acid and digestive juices; the liver makes bile; the pancreas sends juices to the small intestine, where digestion is completed. Finger-like villi in the small intestine absorb the digested food into the blood.

The large intestine absorbs water and some salts from the undigested food. The waste leaves through the anus. Cows and buffaloes (ruminants) swallow grass quickly and later bring it back to chew as cud.

example.q: Why does a roti taste sweet if you chew it slowly for a minute?
steps: Roti is rich in starch.
Saliva contains a substance that breaks starch down into sugar.
Sugar tastes sweet, so the roti starts tasting sweet.
example.answer: Saliva changes some of the starch in the roti into sugar.

learn.hook: Run up the stairs and you start huffing and puffing. Why does your body suddenly want so much more air?
points: Breathing means taking in air (inhaling) and giving out air (exhaling) through the nose and lungs.
Respiration is the process in the cells where food (glucose) is broken down using oxygen to release energy. Carbon dioxide and water are formed.
When we inhale, the diaphragm (a sheet of muscle below the lungs) moves down and the chest expands. When we exhale, it moves up and the chest becomes smaller.
During hard exercise, muscles may not get enough oxygen. Then they break down glucose without oxygen and form lactic acid, which can cause cramps.
Other animals breathe differently: fish use gills, earthworms breathe through their moist skin, insects have tiny holes called spiracles, and frogs use lungs and their moist skin.

example.q: Air you breathe out is bubbled through lime water using a straw, and it turns milky faster than when fresh air is pumped through. What does this show?
steps: Lime water turns milky with carbon dioxide.
Breathed-out air makes it milky faster.
So breathed-out air has more carbon dioxide.
example.answer: Exhaled air contains more carbon dioxide than the air we breathe in.

learn.hook: Your heart is about the size of your fist, yet it beats again and again every minute of your life without taking a holiday!
points: Blood carries oxygen, digested food and other useful things to every part of the body, and takes away wastes like carbon dioxide.
The heart is a muscular organ that pumps blood. The human heart has four chambers.
Arteries carry blood away from the heart. Veins bring blood back to the heart. Tiny tubes called capillaries connect them.
Blood has red blood cells (carry oxygen; their red pigment is haemoglobin), white blood cells (fight germs) and platelets (help blood clot), floating in a liquid called plasma.

learn.hook: A tiny neem seedling grows into a huge tree without eating a single meal. Where does all that food come from?

learn.hook: Plants make oxygen, so do they ever need oxygen themselves? Surprise: yes, all day and all night!
points: Like animals, plants respire: they break down food using oxygen to release energy, giving out carbon dioxide.
Every living part of a plant (roots, stems, leaves, flowers, seeds) respires, day and night.
Leaves take in air through stomata. Roots take oxygen from the air in the spaces between soil particles.
Over-watering fills these spaces with water, so roots cannot get enough air and the plant may die.

Respiration gives out carbon dioxide and releases energy, some as heat.

learn.hook: Your shadow follows you everywhere, but it is short at noon and super-long in the evening. Why does it keep changing size?
points: Light travels in a straight line. That is why we cannot see around a corner.

Transparent materials (clear glass, clean water) let almost all light through. Translucent ones (butter paper, frosted glass) let some light through. Opaque ones (wood, cardboard, your body) let no light through.
A shadow forms when an opaque object blocks light. We need a light source, an opaque object and a surface (screen) to see a shadow.
A shadow is dark whatever the colour of the object. Its size depends on how near the object is to the light: closer to the light gives a bigger shadow.
A pinhole camera shows that light travels in straight lines: the image it forms on its screen is upside down.

example.q: During shadow-puppet play, Arjun moves his hand closer to the torch. What happens to the shadow on the wall?
steps: The torch spreads light outwards in straight lines.

So a bigger area of the wall gets no light.

learn.hook: You can see this page only because light bounces off it into your eyes. That bounce has a name!
points: Reflection is the bouncing back of light when it falls on a surface. Smooth, shiny surfaces like mirrors reflect light very well.
The ray that falls on the mirror is the incident ray; the ray that bounces off is the reflected ray. The normal is an imaginary line at 90° to the mirror at the point where the ray hits.
The angle of incidence is the angle between the incident ray and the normal. The angle of reflection is the angle between the reflected ray and the normal.
Law 1: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.
Law 2: the incident ray, the normal and the reflected ray all lie in the same plane (on the same flat surface).

example.q: A ray of light hits a plane mirror making an angle of 30° with the mirror's surface. What are the angles of incidence and reflection?
steps: The normal is at 90° to the mirror.
Angle of incidence = 90° − 30° = 60° (measured from the normal, not the mirror).
Angle of reflection = angle of incidence = 60°.
example.answer: Both are 60°.

topics.title: Rotation and revolution of the Earth

learn.hook: Right now you are spinning with the Earth and also racing around the Sun, yet you feel perfectly still!
points: The Earth spins on its axis, an imaginary line through the North and South Poles. This spinning is called rotation.
The Earth rotates from west to east, once in about 24 hours. Rotation causes day and night, and makes the Sun appear to rise in the east and set in the west.
The Earth also moves around the Sun in a fixed path called its orbit. This is revolution, and one revolution takes about 365¼ days, which is one year.
The extra quarter days add up, so usually every fourth year has an extra day, 29 February. Such a year has 366 days and is called a leap year.
The Earth's axis is tilted. This tilt, along with revolution, gives us seasons. The Indian astronomer Aryabhata, about 1,500 years ago, wrote that the Earth rotates on its axis.

example.q: Why does the Sun appear to rise in the east every morning?
steps: The Earth rotates from west to east.
So places on the Earth turn towards the Sun from the eastern side first.
To us standing on the ground, the Sun seems to come up from the east.
example.answer: Because the Earth rotates from west to east, the Sun appears to rise in the east.

learn.reallife: When it is morning in India, it is evening or night in the USA, because only half of the rotating Earth faces the Sun at a time.

learn.hook: Diwali is celebrated on a moonless night (amavasya), while many festivals fall on full moon nights (purnima). The Moon has been India's calendar for ages!
points: The Moon does not make its own light. It shines because it reflects sunlight.
Half of the Moon is always lit by the Sun. As the Moon goes around the Earth, we see different amounts of this lit half. These shapes are the phases of the Moon.
New moon (amavasya): the lit half faces away from us, so we cannot see the Moon. Full moon (purnima): we see the whole lit half as a bright disc.
After the new moon the visible part grows (waxing, called Shukla Paksha); after the full moon it shrinks (waning, called Krishna Paksha).
One full cycle of phases takes about 29½ days. The same side of the Moon always faces the Earth.

example.q: Why can't we see the Moon on a new moon night even though it is in the sky?
steps: The Moon shines only by reflecting sunlight.
On new moon day the Moon is between the Earth and the Sun.
Its lit side faces the Sun, and its dark side faces us.
example.answer: Because the side of the Moon facing us is not lit by the Sun.

learn.hook: Imagine the Sun going dark in the middle of the day! A total solar eclipse makes birds settle as if it were dusk, but it lasts only a few minutes.
points: An eclipse happens when the Sun, Earth and Moon come in a straight line and one casts a shadow on the other.
Solar eclipse: the Moon comes between the Sun and the Earth, and the Moon's shadow falls on the Earth. It can happen only on a new moon day.
Lunar eclipse: the Earth comes between the Sun and the Moon, and the Earth's shadow falls on the Moon. It can happen only on a full moon night. In a total lunar eclipse the Moon often looks reddish.
Eclipses do not happen every month, because the Moon's path is slightly tilted compared to the Earth's path, so the three usually do not line up exactly.
Safety: never look at the Sun directly, even during a solar eclipse. Use proper certified solar eclipse glasses. A lunar eclipse is safe to watch with bare eyes.

example.q: Why can a solar eclipse happen only on a new moon day?
steps: In a solar eclipse the Moon must be between the Sun and the Earth.
The Moon is between the Sun and the Earth only around new moon.
So the Moon's shadow can fall on the Earth only then.
example.answer: Because only at new moon is the Moon between the Sun and the Earth.

learn.reallife: Scientists in India travel to places in the path of a total solar eclipse to study the Sun's outer layer, which is visible only when the Moon blocks the bright disc.
